title: Benchmarking Task Takeover Across Agent Handoffs
trick: Freeze one agent's unfinished work, hand six receivers either the transcript tail or an equal-length GPT-4.1-written state sheet, and grade what each recovers and whether it repeats operations already done.
framing_stripped: Called 'the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC-Bench)' for 'task takeover'; it is a paired A/B test of two handoff-message formats (last-N-tokens transcript vs a GPT-4.1-written structured state sheet at the same visible token count) across six receiver models, scored on (a) line-F1 against ContextBench code annotations after a ten-step GPT-5 coding trajectory (300 tasks) and (b) fixed binary checklists over GPT-5.4-generated synthetic continuation tasks (739 tasks: 205 conversational, 386 tool, 148 file-work), with narrative-summary, full-history and privileged target-state arms run for GPT-5.4 only (sec. 3, 4.1, Table 1, Table 3).
method_equations: Continuation score of task $i$ (eq. 1): $s_i(y_i) = \frac{1}{K_i}\sum_{j=1}^{K_i} c_{ij}(y_i)$, where $y_i$ is the receiver's response or interaction trace, $K_i$ the number of binary criteria for task $i$ (17 conversational, 10 tool, 8 file-work; Table 1), and $c_{ij}(y_i) \in \{0,1\}$ is 1 when criterion $j$ is satisfied. Over $N$ tasks (eq. 2): mean score $\bar{s} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} s_i(y_i)$ and all-criteria pass rate $\hat{p} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}[s_i(y_i) = 1]$, with $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator; both reported on a 0-100 scale. Paired context effect (eq. 3): $d_i = s_i(y_i^{(S)}) - s_i(y_i^{(R)})$ and $\widehat{\Delta} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i$, where $y_i^{(S)}$ and $y_i^{(R)}$ are the same receiver's outputs on task $i$ under structured state and recent transcript; for repository tasks $s_i$ is line-F1, $\mathrm{F1} = 2PR/(P+R)$ with $P$ the share of predicted line spans (overlaps merged, at most 12 files and 12 spans per file, unsupported predictions kept in the denominator) that lie in the annotated lines and $R$ the share of annotated lines predicted (App. A). Intervals: 95% percentile bootstrap, 20,000 resamples, resampling whole repositories (repository track) or paired tasks and task families (continuation track) (sec. 4.3). Path retention (Fig. 4): $\rho = |\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{C}| / |\mathcal{A}|$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of annotated target paths that appear in the pre-handoff history and $\mathcal{C}$ the set of paths present in the received context, averaged over the 259 tasks where $|\mathcal{A}| > 0$; observed $\rho = 0.930$ for structured state vs $0.126$ for recent transcripts (sec. 5.3). Context budget: structured state written to 1,600 characters (conversational, tool) or 1,800 (file-work, repository), repository state valid JSON at most 4,000 characters compressing its source at least fivefold; transcript and summary truncated to the same visible o200k_base token count, summaries whitespace-padded after character truncation (App. A).
load_bearing_assumption: That the paired difference $d_i$ isolates the handoff representation: the two messages are 'matched to the structured-state message's visible token count for each task' (sec. 4.1) and differ only in 'the information selected and how it is presented', which the paper concedes it cannot separate ('This comparison concerns the information selected and its presentation together', sec. 5.5); and that 739 continuation tasks generated, screened and diagnostically answered by GPT-5.4 (sec. 3.3), scored by binary criteria whose conversational reference value is 'the earliest matching candidate phrase in the chronological assistant messages' and, 'if none occurs there, the first match in the receiver's continuation supplies it' (App. B), measure continuation rather than schema compliance by the generator's own family. If the first fails, 'structured state helps' is 'GPT-4.1 selected better facts'; if the second fails, the GPT-5.4 lead on the continuation track (92.76 mean, 52.1% pass, Table 2) is a generator-receiver match.
weakest_component: The headline pass-rate gain is a property of the criterion set, and the paper shows it: Table 4 reports structured-state-minus-transcript completion differences of +7.44 to +12.18 points for all six receivers under the benchmark criteria, but when one criterion is added ('+ status match adds order-status matching in the tool-observation field') the sign flips for five of six (Claude +9.07 to -9.88, DeepSeek +12.18 to -7.58, Qwen +10.55 to -6.09, Gemini +12.18 to -3.92, Kimi +9.07 to -5.28; only GPT-5.4 stays positive at +6.09), with four of the five negative intervals crossing zero. A critic attacks this first because it means 'structured state improves continuation performance for most models' (abstract) depends on which binary checks the authors kept. Behind it: (1) the same model family (GPT-5.4) writes the synthetic tasks, screens them and leads the track; (2) the structured-state writer gets the output-field names for file-work tasks and 284 of 739 narrative summaries are truncated, so the 5.42-point state-over-summary gap is 3.04 on the 429 clean tasks (Table 8); (3) the action-level finding is 2 repeats out of 114 continuations (sec. 5.4), both on one task; (4) effects on the 0-100 mean are 3-5 points on a scale where the transcript arm already scores 77.96-89.73 (Table 2); (5) handoff messages are written by a single fixed model (GPT-4.1) under one prompt, so 'structured state' is one instance of the format, not the format.
regime: Receivers: gpt-5.4, claude-sonnet-5, deepseek-v3.2, qwen3.5-plus-2026-02-15, gemini-3.5-flash-lite, kimi-k2-250905; source agent GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07); context writer GPT-4.1; temperature 0, top-$p$ 1, output limits 1,536 tokens (continuation) and 1,024 (repository); GPT-5 and Gemini at minimal reasoning, Qwen with thinking disabled (App. A). Repository track: 300 tasks, 38 repositories, 8 languages, GPT-5 histories from CodeTraceBench (193 OpenHands, 52 SWE-agent, 55 mini-SWE-agent trajectories), handoff after ten complete action-observation pairs; 217 tasks with annotated paths earlier-only, 42 still-recent, 41 not observed (sec. 3.1). Continuation track: 739 synthetic tasks from 1,130 GPT-5.4 candidates (205 of 250 conversational, 386 of 560 tool, 148 of 320 file-work; 5, 7 and 5 scenario families), receiver continues through prescribed messages with at most four model calls on tool tasks; receivers 'do not modify files or execute tests' on file-work tasks (sec. 3.2, App. A). Handoff message size about 1,600-1,800 characters, repository state up to 4,000 characters. Pass-rate band: line-F1 0.031-0.147 (transcript) and 0.189-0.263 (state); continuation mean 77.96-89.73 (transcript), 79.45-92.76 (state), 88.90-94.51 (full history); all-criteria pass 27.5-44.7% (transcript), 36.5-52.1% (state), 42.2-57.9% (full); GPT-5.4 with privileged target state 98.30 / 85.3% (Table 2, Table 3). API-only compute, no training.
information_asymmetry: (1) Message vs continuation (the ruler question for L4 and CL-W43-05). The paper grades the receiver's output given the message and grades the message itself only by path retention (annotated paths kept: 93.0% state vs 12.6% transcript over 259 tasks, Fig. 4). Per-entry provenance of the state sheet is never computed although it is computable: GPT-4.1 writes the sheet 'from the task description and observable history, without access to reference annotations or target values' (sec. 4.1), so every entry either matches an observation in the source history or does not, and that label plus the criterion-level outcome exists for 739 x 6 continuations. CL-W43-05's mechanism (unsourced entries drive post-boundary failure) is therefore neither tested nor contradicted here; what the paper does settle is the complementary cell: when the completion record is present and sourced in both messages (19 tasks x 6 receivers), 2 of 114 structured-state continuations still repeat the operation (sec. 5.4), completed-action reporting rises 77.3% to 87.3% while the update-call-count criterion is flat at 95.5% to 95.3% (App. B.1), and the paper's own diagnostic is 'was the completion record missing, or did the receiver repeat the operation despite having that record?' (sec. 6). A handoff-quality ruler built on provenance alone cannot see that cell; a ruler needs a message axis (what is in the sheet and whether it is sourced) and a use axis (what the receiver does with a sourced entry), and this paper supplies the second only. (2) Message-alone vs message-with-receiver. The authors argue the ruler must be receiver-conditional: 536 of 739 continuation tasks improve for at least one receiver but 48 for all six; 231 of 300 repository tasks improve for at least one, 91 for all (Fig. 6); Kimi's tool-state score falls 9.43 points under structured state while its conversational score rises 6.05 (Fig. 3); 'The usefulness of a handoff context therefore depends on the receiving model even when the underlying task and source history are held fixed' (sec. 5.2). Any message-intrinsic quality score is refuted as a sufficient predictor by these numbers. (3) Writer at handoff time vs the remaining task. The writer does not know what the receiver will need; the paper measures the price: full history gives GPT-5.4 a 57.9% pass rate, privileged target state 85.3% (Table 3), so 27.4 points separate 'everything that happened' from 'what matters', and no handoff message can close more than the history-to-target gap. This ceiling is computed for one receiver only and never for the structured-state arm; the ratio (state gain) / (target-state minus transcript) is the natural efficiency of a handoff format and is absent. (4) Report vs action. Criteria on reported fields move (T7 +10.0 points, F2 test observations 12.6% to 38.9%) while criteria on actions or on reported test success do not (T9 flat; F5 68.0% to 66.2%; Table 5): a report-level grade overstates action-level continuation, and the file-work track is report-only by construction. (5) Single vs chained handoff. 'one receiver's output becomes part of the next receiver's input' is named as the open extension (sec. 6); the benchmark has one handoff and no measurement of how an incorrect completion record propagates. (6) Mean vs pass. Kimi gains 67 all-criteria passes while losing 3.33 mean points (sec. 5.6): the two aggregate rulers disagree on the direction of the effect for one receiver, so the choice of aggregate is itself a design decision a handoff ruler must pre-register.
occupies: Now published: a 1,039-task handoff benchmark (300 ContextBench-annotated repository tasks at a ten-step GPT-5 handoff; 739 GPT-5.4-generated continuation tasks with fixed binary criteria) showing that an equal-visible-token GPT-4.1-written structured state beats the transcript tail on line-F1 for all six receivers (+0.114 to +0.162, all repository-level intervals above zero; +0.132 to +0.189 on the 217 earlier-only tasks), on all-criteria pass rate for all six (+7.44 to +12.18 points under the benchmark criteria), and on mean score for five of six; beats a narrative summary for GPT-5.4 (+5.42, +3.04 on 429 untruncated non-file tasks); that the track leaders differ (Claude and Gemini on recovery, GPT-5.4 on continuation); that path retention is 93.0% vs 12.6%; and that a present completion record is still re-executed in 2 of 114 continuations. For a handoff-quality ruler it settles that (a) the receiver must be part of the ruler (48 of 739 tasks improve for all six), (b) report-level and action-level criteria diverge, and (c) the full-history-to-target-state gap (57.9% to 85.3% for GPT-5.4) bounds what any message can add; it leaves open per-entry provenance of the handoff message (CL-W43-05's axis, untested here), a criterion set that does not flip sign under one added check, chained handoffs, and any writer other than GPT-4.1 under one prompt.

neighbors.title: Handoff Debt: The Rediscovery Cost When Coding Agents Take Over Interrupted Tasks
neighbors.trick: Interrupt a coding agent at fixed points, freeze the repository, and have successor agents resume under four views (repository only, raw trace, summary notes, structured notes); context-bearing handoffs cut median agent events 20-59% and prompt tokens 42-63% while solved rate moves little; this card's paper grades what the receiver recovers and repeats rather than what the takeover costs.

neighbors.title: Evaluating Performance Drift from Model Switching in Multi-Turn LLM Systems
neighbors.trick: Run a prefix model for early turns and a different suffix model for the last turn, compare against no switch with paired bootstrap, and decompose the drift into per-model prefix influence and suffix susceptibility (about 70% of variance); the handoff there is a raw dialogue prefix, with no compressed message and no action state.

neighbors.title: Reach or Solve? Deep Diving into Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs
neighbors.trick: Replay one checkpoint's history under another so that 'reaching a state a fixed number of actions from success' and 'solving from a cloned copy of that state' are scored separately; the handoff is the full replayed history, used to decompose RL gains, not a lossy message.

neighbors.title: Slipstream: Trajectory-Grounded Compaction Validation for Long-Horizon Agents
neighbors.trick: Run the compactor in parallel with the agent continuing on the uncompacted context, then have a judge check the candidate summary against the agent's actual next steps for forward intent and key facts; a per-message validation signal at write time, where this card's paper measures the message only through the receiver's downstream score.

neighbors.title: ContextBench: A Benchmark for Context Retrieval in Coding Agents
neighbors.trick: Annotate 1,136 issue-resolution tasks across 66 repositories with human gold code contexts and track context recall, precision and efficiency along the agent's trajectory; this card's paper borrows its annotations as the withheld reference for the repository track's line-F1.

theme_fit.why: a handoff message (transcript tail vs structured state vs narrative summary) written by one agent for another is measured by what the receiver recovers and does; the lane's own object, in the measurement register, with the per-entry provenance axis of CL-W43-05 left uncomputed

benchmark validity is on display: a one-criterion change flips the headline completion gain for five of six receivers (Table 4), mean and pass rate disagree for Kimi, and the task generator (GPT-5.4) is the leading receiver; receiver sensitivity (48 of 739 tasks improve for all six) is an attribution question
handoffs are named in the lane but the paper trains nothing; the privileged target-state arm (85.3% vs 57.9% for full history) is the only hint of a learnable target for a handoff writer

limitations_as_complaints: My pipeline chains several handoffs and an incorrect completion record in one message is inherited by every later receiver; this benchmark measures one handoff and says so: 'The single-handoff setting studied here provides a starting point for examining such errors' (sec. 6).

I cannot tell from this whether a structured state wins because of what it keeps or because of how it is laid out: 'This comparison concerns the information selected and its presentation together' (sec. 5.5), and the state-over-summary comparison is further confounded because 'Some narrative summaries are truncated to meet the token budget, and structured-state preparation additionally receives output-field names for file-work tasks' (sec. 5.5), shrinking the gap from 5.42 to 3.04 points on the 429 clean tasks (Table 8).

The file-work track grades a progress report, not a resumed edit, and even the best message leaves most test observations out: 'The evaluated output is this report; receivers do not modify files or execute tests' (sec. 3.2) and 'Even with structured state, detailed test reports remain incomplete on many tasks' (App. B.1; test-observation criterion 12.6% to 38.9%, Table 5).
